content: 1. The use of tamponade devices, including both improvised and low-cost purpose-designed devices, is being evaluated for their effectiveness in reducing maternal morbidity and mortality associated with postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). 2. The comparative effectiveness of uterine balloon tamponades versus other tamponade interventions, such as suction devices, is being assessed in terms of their ability to reduce PPH-related maternal morbidity and mortality. 3. The safety and comparative effectiveness of various tamponade devices for treating refractory PPH during cesarean sections are being investigated, with a focus on their impact on maternal morbidity and mortality. 4. The most effective methods for training and ensuring competency in the use of uterine balloon tamponades are being explored to optimize their application in clinical practice. 5. Implementing evidence-based recommendations for uterine balloon tamponade use requires resources for sustainable procurement and storage of these devices, as well as the necessary commodities for first-line PPH treatment. 6. Updating training curricula and providing education on these recommendations can enhance their impact and facilitate their implementation in clinical settings. 7. Standardizing care by incorporating these recommendations into existing intrapartum and immediate postpartum care packages can encourage healthcare providers to adopt evidence-based practices. 8. Potential barriers to implementing these recommendations include a lack of skilled human resources, resistance to changing from non-evidence-based to evidence-based practices, and insufficient understanding of the recommended interventions among healthcare personnel and system managers. 9. Additional challenges include inadequate infrastructure to support interventions, lack of essential equipment and supplies, ineffective mechanisms for identifying PPH cases, and insufficient health information systems to document and monitor recommended practices. 10. Strategies to address these barriers and facilitate implementation are outlined in the guideline's implementation considerations. 11. Monitoring and evaluating the implementation and impact of these recommendations will occur at health service, country, and regional levels as part of broader efforts to improve maternal and newborn care quality. 12. WHO's Standards for improving quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities provides prioritized measures to define quality-of-care criteria and indicators aligned with local targets. 13. Data on the implementation of these recommendations will be collected and evaluated in collaboration with WHO's monitoring and evaluation teams to assess their impact on national policies. 14. Interrupted time series, clinical audits, or criterion-based audits may be used to gather relevant data on the use of interventions outlined in the guideline. 15. WHO has developed specific guidance for evaluating the quality of care for severe maternal complications, including PPH, using near-miss and criterion-based clinical audit concepts. 16. The Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) reviews WHO's maternal and perinatal health recommendations annually to prioritize new and existing questions for development and updating. 17. This recommendation will be reviewed and prioritized by the Executive GSG, and updates may occur if new evidence emerges that could impact the current evidence base. 18. If no new evidence is identified, the recommendation may be revalidated. Concerns about the validity of the recommendation should be promptly communicated to guideline implementers. 19. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to include in updated recommendations. 20. The effectiveness and safety of introducing uterine balloon tamponades, such as condom-catheter devices, for PPH management have been studied in various settings, including secondary-level hospitals in Uganda, Egypt, and Senegal. 21. WHO's guidance emphasizes the importance of aligning quality-of-care measures with locally agreed targets to improve maternal and newborn care outcomes.
